22.title: Marcus doesn't want to get up
22.word: Marcus doesn't want to get up
22.hook: the emperor argues with himself under the blankets: was I made to lie here warm?
22.carry: up, to do a human's work
22.howItsDone: Many people who practice Stoicism today begin the morning with a short reflection, often reading Marcus Aurelius, and remind themselves of the day's duties and the kind of person they want to be in them.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rumi, and camp one closed with twenty-one words. Your line was meet me there. Did you take one small step toward someone? Day twenty-two.
screen: `RUMI — MEET ME THERE.`

segments.voice: Camp two. The stories. From today, the words become people, and first up are the Stoics, the philosophers of ancient Greece and Rome who taught that a good life is built from what you do with what happens to you. Picture a tent, maybe somewhere near the Danube, in the second century. It's cold. It's early. The most powerful man in the world is lying under his blankets, and he does not want to get up. He is Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome. And instead of just getting up, or just staying there, he does something odd. He argues with himself about it, in writing.
screen: `CAMP TWO: THE STORIES.` → `A COLD TENT BY THE DANUBE.` → `THE EMPEROR STAYS IN BED.`

segments.voice: Marcus kept a private notebook, the one we met back in camp one, and much of it was probably written on military campaigns in his last decade. Book five opens right there, under the blankets. In George Long's translation, he tells himself that when he rises unwillingly, he should remember: "I am rising to the work of a human being." Then he asks the question in today's hook: "Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?" And then, and this is the best part, he answers himself back. But it's more pleasant here. As if the emperor of Rome is haggling with his own pillow. So he looks outside. The little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, he says, are all busy doing their part to keep the world in order. And you, a human being, won't do yours? It's easy to hear that as a scolding. But notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say get up because you'll be rich, or famous, or because the empire needs you. He says get up because there's a human's work to do, and you're a human. Being kind, being fair, being useful to the people around you: for a Stoic, that was the job description. The alarm isn't a punishment. It's a reminder of what you're for. And here's what makes this story worth telling. This isn't a sage who never struggled. It's a tired man, winning a very small argument, one morning at a time, and writing it down so he'd remember next time.
screen: `BOOK FIVE STARTS UNDER THE BLANKETS.` · `MADE TO KEEP MYSELF WARM?` · `THE ANTS, THE SPIDERS, THE BEES.` · `A SMALL ARGUMENT, EVERY MORNING.` · then, large: `THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.`

segments.voice: From today, the bell gives you two minutes. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture tomorrow morning: the room, the light, the sound of the alarm. Feel the pull to stay under the covers. It's real, and it's allowed. Now picture yourself getting up at the first alarm, just once. Feet on the floor. And ask Marcus's question: what's the human's work waiting for me today? Let one thing come to mind. A person to be kind to, a job to do well. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Marcus doesn't want to get up. An emperor, arguing with his own blankets, and reminding himself what a human being is for.
screen: `MARCUS DOESN'T WANT TO GET UP — today's word`.

23.title: The master and the leg
23.hook: enslaved, Epictetus warns his master he'll break his leg, it breaks, and he says calmly "didn't I tell you?"
23.howItsDone: Stoic practice sorts troubles into what is in our power and what is not, and puts effort only into the first: our own judgments, choices and responses.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus doesn't want to get up: the emperor arguing with his blankets. Your line was up, to do a human's work. Did you get up at the first alarm? Day twenty-three.
screen: `UP, TO DO A HUMAN'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Yesterday an emperor. Today, a man at the very bottom of the same empire. He was born in a town in what's now Turkey, and he was born enslaved. The only name we have for him, Epictetus, is a Greek word for acquired. Bought. His owner was a wealthy man in Rome, himself a former slave of the emperor Nero's household. And one day, so the story goes, the owner starts twisting Epictetus's leg. Hard. For no reason we're told. And Epictetus, instead of crying out, looks at him and speaks.
screen: `THE BOTTOM OF THE SAME EMPIRE.` → `HIS NAME MEANS ACQUIRED.` → `THE MASTER TWISTS HIS LEG.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as it comes down to us. Epictetus says, quietly: you're going to break it. The master keeps twisting. The leg breaks. And Epictetus says, calmly: didn't I tell you it would break? That's it. No scream, no curse. Now, honesty about the source. This story isn't from Epictetus himself. It comes from an ancient writer named Celsus, who told it in a book attacking Christianity, and we only have it because a Christian scholar, Origen, quoted Celsus in order to answer him. Another ancient source says Epictetus's lameness came from illness, not cruelty. So we can't be sure it happened. But we know Epictetus was lame, and we know what he taught about it. In George Long's translation of his handbook: "Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will." And the handbook's first line: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." A twisted leg is not in your power, if someone stronger is doing the twisting. What you say while it happens, that part may still be yours. Please hear what this story doesn't mean. It doesn't mean cruelty is fine, or that pain doesn't hurt, or that someone being harmed should just keep quiet. If it happened, it was wrong. The story is about something smaller and stranger: that even at the very bottom, with no power at all, a person can still choose the voice they answer in. Epictetus spent the rest of his life teaching that.
screen: `YOU'RE GOING TO BREAK IT.` · `A STORY TOLD BY A CRITIC.` · `IMPEDIMENT TO THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.` · `CRUELTY IS STILL WRONG.` · then, large: `THE VOICE YOU ANSWER IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then gently notice one pain you can't change today. A sore back. A diagnosis. A person who won't change. A loss. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just let it be there, and breathe beside it. Then ask quietly: what part of this is mine? Maybe only the voice you answer it in. Rest with that for a while. If it's too much today, just come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The master and the leg. An enslaved man, a broken leg, and a calm answer: didn't I tell you?

segments.voice: Your line: said calmly. Today, when something you can't change goes wrong, notice the voice you answer in. Choose it, once. Day twenty-three.

24.title: Epictetus goes free
24.hook: freed, he teaches in Rome, is banished with all philosophers by Domitian, and opens a school at Nicopolis around 93 CE
24.howItsDone: Modern Stoics often keep a short written list of what is truly in their power, their own choices and responses, and read the Discourses and Handbook of Epictetus as a daily guide.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the master and the leg, and a man who answered calmly. Your line was said calmly. When something you couldn't change went wrong, what voice did you answer in? Day twenty-four.
screen: `THE MASTER AND THE LEG — SAID CALMLY.`

segments.voice: We left Epictetus enslaved, with a leg that would never work properly again. Here's what happened next. At some point, and we don't know exactly when or how, he was set free. He'd already been studying philosophy while enslaved, with a Roman Stoic teacher named Musonius Rufus. Now he started teaching it himself, in Rome. A lame, formerly enslaved man, teaching the sons of the powerful how to live. And then the emperor Domitian decided philosophers were a nuisance and threw them all out of the city.
screen: `SET FREE, SOMEHOW.` → `A LAME MAN TEACHING IN ROME.` → `THE EMPEROR THROWS THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome; historians still debate the exact year. Epictetus lost his city, his students, whatever he'd built. So he went across the sea to Nicopolis, a town on the western coast of Greece, and opened a school. And people came. Young men traveled, some of them a long way, to sit on hard benches and be questioned by this lame teacher. As far as we know, Epictetus never wrote a book. We have his teaching only because one student, Arrian, wrote down what he said, and later published it as the Discourses and a short handbook. Through them, you can hear him in class. In one passage, he imagines a tyrant threatening him. You'll chain me? You can chain my leg. But my will, not even Zeus himself can take that. In another, he tells how a thief stole the iron lamp from his little shrine at home. His response: next time I'll buy a clay one. And then the twist: the thief lost more than I did. He paid for a lamp by becoming a thief. The Greek word he kept coming back to was prohairesis, usually translated will, or choice: your power to decide how you'll meet what happens. Epictetus had been owned, lamed, freed, exiled. Everything outside kept being taken. And that's the point of the story. The school at Nicopolis was real, with benches and walls. But the school he actually taught was one you carry inside. No emperor can banish it.
screen: `EXILED BY DOMITIAN.` · `A SCHOOL AT NICOPOLIS.` · `YOU CAN CHAIN MY LEG.` · `THE THIEF LOST MORE.` · then, large: `THE SCHOOL IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then ask yourself: what's one thing no one can take from me? Not an object. Something inside. The way you treat people. Your sense of humor. A memory. What you choose to pay attention to. Let an answer come, and rest with it. If you have paper nearby, after the bell, write it down in one line. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus goes free. Freed, then exiled, and still teaching: a school at Nicopolis, and one you carry inside.
screen: `EPICTETUS GOES FREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the school is inside. Today, write down the one thing no one can take, and put it somewhere you'll see it. Day twenty-four.

25.title: Zeno's shipwreck
25.hook: a merchant loses his cargo of purple dye off Athens and wanders into a bookshop
25.carry: I sailed well when I was wrecked
25.howItsDone: Stoics practice looking at a setback as material to work with rather than simply a disaster, asking what response is still in their power after the loss.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus goes free, and opens a school no emperor could close. Your line was the school is inside. What did you write down that no one can take? Day twenty-five.
screen: `EPICTETUS GOES FREE — THE SCHOOL IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: We've met two Stoics: an emperor and an enslaved teacher. Today, the man who started it all, centuries before either of them. His name was Zeno, from Citium, a city on the island of Cyprus. He was a merchant, carrying a cargo of purple dye from Phoenicia. And somewhere off the coast near Athens, the ship went down. The cargo, the fortune, gone into the sea. Zeno made it to shore with, as far as we know, nothing.
screen: `THE MAN WHO STARTED IT ALL.` → `A CARGO OF PURPLE DYE.` → `THE SHIP GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: Our source for this is Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote lives of the Greek philosophers centuries after Zeno, collecting stories from older books, some of them already disagreeing. So think of this as the story the ancient world told about Zeno, not a court record. Here's how it goes. Shipwrecked, broke, around thirty years old, Zeno walks up from the harbor into Athens. He doesn't know anyone. He wanders into a bookseller's shop and sits down. And the bookseller is reading aloud, or Zeno picks up, a book about Socrates, written by one of Socrates's students. Zeno is hooked. Something in the way Socrates lived, questioning everything, owning almost nothing, unafraid, hits him right in the chest. He's lost everything he owned, and on the same trip, he finds the thing he'll spend the rest of his life on. Years later, according to Diogenes, Zeno looked back on the wreck and said something like: I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked. Another version has him thanking Fortune for driving him to philosophy. Either way, the man who lost a fortune at sea went on to found a school that would reach an emperor in his tent, an enslaved teacher in Nicopolis, and people reading the Stoics on their phones today. Now, gently. Not every loss sends you somewhere good, and nobody should tell a grieving person that everything happens for a reason. The Stoics didn't say the wreck was good. They said what you do after the wreck is still yours. Zeno's cargo sank. Zeno walked into a bookshop.
screen: `A STORY TOLD CENTURIES LATER.` · `BROKE, IN A BOOKSHOP.` · `A BOOK ABOUT SOCRATES.` · `NOT EVERY LOSS IS A GIFT.` · then, large: `I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then look back over your life for one loss that, in the end, sent you somewhere good. A job that ended. A plan that fell through. A move you didn't want. Not the worst loss, just one where you can see the bookshop now. Let it come back: what sank, and where you washed up. Notice the thread between them. If no loss like that comes, that's all right. Just rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Zeno's shipwreck. A merchant loses his fortune at sea, walks into a bookshop, and finds his life's work.
screen: `ZENO'S SHIPWRECK — today's word`.

26.title: Follow that man
26.hook: Zeno asks the bookseller where men like Socrates can be found, and Crates the Cynic walks past
26.howItsDone: In the ancient schools, people learned philosophy by attaching themselves to a living teacher and following them about; many people today still seek out a teacher or a community to learn from in person.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zeno's shipwreck: a fortune lost at sea, and a bookshop. Your line was I sailed well when I was wrecked. Did you remember a loss that sent you somewhere good? Day twenty-six.
screen: `ZENO'S SHIPWRECK — I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: We left Zeno in a bookshop in Athens, broke, shipwrecked, and completely hooked on a book about Socrates. But Socrates had been dead for generations. So Zeno looks up from the page and asks the bookseller a question. Where can I find men like this? Real ones. Alive. And right at that moment, as if the story had been waiting for its cue, a strange figure walks past the shop door. And the bookseller points at him and says three words. Follow that man.
screen: `SOCRATES WAS LONG DEAD.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THIS?` → `A STRANGE FIGURE WALKS PAST.`

segments.voice: The man walking past was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. The Cynics were the punk rockers of ancient Greece. They owned almost nothing, slept in public, said exactly what they thought, and mocked anything fake. The name comes from the Greek for dog-like, because they lived as openly as dogs. Crates had been born rich, in Thebes, and given his wealth away. Ancient writers say people called him the door-opener, because he walked into any house he liked and gave the family advice, and they were glad to see him. A woman named Hipparchia, from a wealthy family, fell in love with him and chose his life of the road over her comfortable one, and became a philosopher in her own right. So Zeno followed. He became Crates's student. But there was a problem. Zeno was shy, and the Cynics were shameless on purpose. So Diogenes Laërtius tells this story. Crates hands Zeno a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through a busy part of Athens. Zeno, embarrassed, tries to hide it under his cloak. Crates cracks the pot with his staff. Soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno runs. And Crates calls after him, roughly: why are you running, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Embarrassment, Crates was saying, isn't harm. But look at how it all began. A curious question, asked out loud. A stranger walking past. And the nerve to get up from a bookseller's bench and follow him out the door.
screen: `THE CYNICS: DOG-LIKE, AND PROUD.` · `CRATES, THE DOOR-OPENER.` · `A POT OF LENTIL SOUP.` · `EMBARRASSMENT ISN'T HARM.` · then, large: `FOLLOW THAT MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then ask yourself Zeno's question, in your own words: where can I find more of this? Something you've been curious about lately, a subject, a skill, a kind of person you'd like to learn from. Let it come. Then picture the bookseller pointing. Where's the door? Who's walking past? A book, a class, a person you could ask. Just notice where the finger points. The bell holds the time.
Follow that man. A bookseller points, a Cynic walks by, and a shipwrecked merchant gets up and follows.

27.title: The painted porch
27.hook: Zeno teaches in a public colonnade, and the school takes its name from the porch
27.howItsDone: Stoicism has always been practiced in ordinary life rather than apart from it: its followers aim to be steady and just in public roles, at work and in the family.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, follow that man: a bookseller pointed, and Zeno followed a Cynic out the door. Your line was follow that man. Which curiosity did you give five minutes to? Day twenty-seven.
screen: `FOLLOW THAT MAN.`

segments.voice: Zeno spent years learning from Crates and other teachers in Athens. Then, sometime around the year three hundred BCE, he started teaching himself. But he had no money left, no building, no school. So where do you teach, when you have nothing? Zeno picked a spot right in the middle of the city. Not behind a wall, not in a private garden. On the edge of the marketplace, the agora, where everyone walked past all day long. A long covered walkway with columns, painted inside with huge famous pictures. The Greeks had a word for a porch like that. Today's word is stoa.
screen: `NO MONEY, NO BUILDING.` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE CITY.` → `A COVERED WALKWAY WITH COLUMNS.`

segments.voice: A stoa was a colonnade: a long roof held up by a row of columns, open on one side, where people could get out of the sun or the rain. Athens had several. The one Zeno chose was called the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch, because its walls held great paintings by famous artists, including a scene of the Battle of Marathon, the day Athens had fought off a Persian invasion. So picture it. Merchants shouting in the market. People sheltering from the heat. Travelers staring at the paintings. And a thin, serious man from Cyprus walking up and down between the columns, talking, while anyone who wanted to could stop and listen. Diogenes Laërtius says that at first his followers were called Zenonians, after him. But the name that stuck was the place. People who met at the porch. The Stoics. Other schools in Athens met in different kinds of places. Plato's Academy was in a grove outside the city walls. Epicurus gathered his friends in a private garden. Each place suited its school. The Stoics were named for a public porch in the busiest part of town, and the fit is almost too good. Their whole teaching was about living well in the middle of ordinary life: in the market, the law court, the family, the army. Not by escaping the world, but in it. Two thousand three hundred years later, the name of a building is still the name of a way of life. Every time someone says stoic, they're pointing, without knowing it, at a painted porch in the middle of a crowd.
screen: `A LONG ROOF ON A ROW OF COLUMNS.` · `PAINTINGS OF MARATHON.` · `ZENONIANS, THEN STOICS.` · `LIVING WELL IN THE MIDDLE OF LIFE.` · then, large: `WISDOM IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you're somewhere public right now, a bus, a cafe, a park, stay there, and sit with your eyes open or half closed. If you're at home, picture a busy street you know. Let the noise and the movement go on around you. You don't have to escape it to be steady. Let people pass. Let sounds come and go. Breathe in the middle of it, the way Zeno taught in the middle of the market. The bell holds the time.
Stoa. A porch with columns, open to the street, and the place that gave the Stoics their name.
screen: `STOA — today's word`.

trapdoor: what you thought: stoic means keeping a stiff upper lip.
what it means: people who met at a public porch, and a way of living well in the middle of ordinary life.

28.title: Cleanthes carries water
28.hook: the boxer who drew water at night so he could study by day
28.howItsDone: Stoics treat ordinary tasks as a place to practice virtue, doing humble work carefully and without resentment; Cleanthes's life is still told as the example.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: stoa, the painted porch that named a school. Your line was wisdom in the open. Did you sit somewhere public and stay steady in the middle of it? Day twenty-eight, the end of week four.
screen: `STOA — WISDOM IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Somewhere in the crowd at the painted porch, listening to Zeno, is a big man with a boxer's shoulders. His name is Cleanthes. He came to Athens, the story goes, with almost no money in his pocket. He wanted to study philosophy all day. But he had to eat. So every night, while Athens slept, he worked in the gardens around the city, hauling water up from the wells by hand, bucket after bucket, so the plants would live. And every morning, tired, hands raw, he walked to the porch and sat down to listen.
screen: `A BOXER AT THE PAINTED PORCH.` → `NO MONEY IN HIS POCKET.` → `WATER AT NIGHT, WISDOM BY DAY.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius tells the rest, and it gets better. People noticed this strong young man who studied all day and never seemed to work. How was he living? He was summoned before the city's council to explain himself. Cleanthes brought witnesses: the gardener whose water he drew, and a woman whose grain he ground. The council was so impressed they voted him a gift of money. And Zeno, his teacher, told him not to take it. The Athenians started calling him the well-drawer. He was, the story says, a slow learner, and other students called him the donkey. His reply: fine, then I'm the only one strong enough to carry Zeno's load. He couldn't afford writing material, so he wrote his notes on oyster shells and the flat shoulder bones of oxen. And here's the ending. When Zeno died, the man who took over the school wasn't the quickest student. It was Cleanthes. The water carrier. The lesson people have drawn from his life is simple. No task is beneath a person who does it well. The humble work and the high work are the same work, done by the same character. And that's week four. Marcus doesn't want to get up. The master and the leg. Epictetus goes free. Zeno's shipwreck. Follow that man. Stoa. And Cleanthes, carrying water. An emperor, an enslaved man, a shipwrecked merchant, a Cynic, and a boxer with a bucket. The Stoics woke up.
screen: `HAULED BEFORE THE COUNCIL.` · `THE DONKEY CARRIES ZENO'S LOAD.` · `NOTES ON OYSTER SHELLS.` · `THE WATER CARRIER LEADS THE SCHOOL.` · then, large: `NO TASK IS BENEATH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then think of one humble task waiting for you today. The dishes, the laundry, taking out the trash, answering the boring email. Picture yourself doing it slowly and well, the way Cleanthes drew water: one bucket, then the next. No resentment, no hurry. Just the task and your hands. Notice how it changes when it isn't beneath you. The bell holds the time.
Cleanthes carries water. A boxer who hauled water at night so he could study by day, and went on to lead the Stoic school.
screen: `CLEANTHES CARRIES WATER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: carry the water. Today, do one humble task as well as you can. That's week four: seven stories, and the Stoics are awake. Day twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 28 COUNTS. WEEK FOUR DONE.` → `TOMORROW: CATO'S LAST NIGHT.`
